lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
For Jordan’s cardboard prototype, write the action you would measure or try for each criterion: holds 8 pencils, fits the 15 cm desk corner, and has no sharp edges. Say what result you would write down.

FEEDBACK
Count pencils after one gentle nudge, measure the base in centimetres against 15 cm, and trace every edge. The pencil result is a number out of 8. The corner result is two measurements compared with 15 cm by 15 cm. The edge result is smooth or scratch for each edge. “It seems fine” is not a recorded result. Do the tests with the prototype already made; do not cut during the test.

WATCH FOR
Saying the prototype passed after a glance, without counting, measuring or tracing an edge. A glance has no number and no yes-or-no record, so nobody can repeat it. Write the action and the result for each criterion before you decide how good the design is.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Plan three tests for a cardboard bookend that must hold three paperbacks upright, fit a shelf end, and have no sharp edge. Say what you would count or measure, and what result you would write. Do not reuse the pencil count of 8 or the 15 cm desk corner.

Write a short reflection naming one observation, criterion or step you corrected and why.

Edges: trace every edge with a fingertip and write “scratch” or “smooth” for each edge. Record the result beside the criterion before you judge the whole design. Scissors stay down during the test. Look at each observation, source detail or example that carries the idea.
teaching.rule: Make the technology idea visible: name the observation, source or example you used and say why it supports the claim.
teaching.why: This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen, measured or tested against criteria.

teaching.feedback: Count pencils after one gentle nudge, measure the base in centimetres against 15 cm, and trace every edge. The pencil result is a number out of 8. The corner result is two measurements compared with 15 cm by 15 cm. The edge result is smooth or scratch for each edge. “It seems fine” is not a recorded result. Do the tests with the prototype already made; do not cut during the test.
teaching.fix: Correct the claim, criteria use or method, not just the neatness of the diagram.
teaching.guided_attempt: Describe why the warned-against claim fails, then write a corrected claim with evidence.
teaching.misconception: Changing the wording without repairing the evidence does not fix the error. Saying the prototype passed after a glance, without counting, measuring or tracing an edge. A glance has no number and no yes-or-no record, so nobody can repeat it. Write the action and the result for each criterion before you decide how good the design is.

teaching.rule: Use an intentionally incorrect claim as a comparison. Name its specific technology error, then show the corrected evidence-based claim.
teaching.why: This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen, measured or tested against criteria.

teaching.feedback: The new example should use the same technology idea as the model, but contain different evidence.
teaching.fix: Correct the claim, criteria use or method, not just the neatness of the diagram.
teaching.guided_attempt: Inquire into or describe one fresh example that uses the same skill and write a short evidence-based reason.
teaching.misconception: Repeating the worked example cannot show transfer to new evidence.
teaching.model: Testing a prototype means trying each criterion in a way someone else could repeat. For Jordan, three tests match the three criteria. Count how many of 8 pencils stay in after one gentle nudge. Measure the base in centimetres and compare it with the 15 cm by 15 cm corner. Trace every edge with a fingertip and note any point that scratches. A nudge is a small sideways push with one finger, not a throw. Looking at the tube and saying “it seems fine” is not a test, because no result was recorded. Now choose a different example to show you can transfer the idea.
teaching.rule: Use the same technology idea on a new place, person, source or context, not a copy of the worked example. Review accuracy of evidence.
teaching.why: This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen, measured or tested against criteria.
